title: Garments for the Priests
summary: God tells Moses to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests and to have skilled craftsmen make holy garments for them. The high priest's clothing is described in detail: the ephod with two shoulder stones engraved with Israel's tribes, the breastpiece of judgment with twelve gems and the Urim and Thummim, a blue robe hemmed with pomegranates and gold bells, and a gold plate inscribed HOLY TO THE LORD. Aaron's sons receive tunics, sashes, headbands, and linen undergarments.
story: At Mount Sinai God has made his covenant with Israel (chapter 24) and has begun giving Moses the plans for the tabernacle, the portable tent where he will live among his people (chapters 25-27). Now the instructions turn from the building to the people who will serve in it. A holy God dwelling in the middle of a sinful people raises an obvious question: who can come near? The answer given here is a priesthood, mediators who represent the people before God. This chapter clothes them; chapter 29 describes how they are to be ordained. The irony is sharp in the larger story: while Moses is on the mountain receiving these plans, Aaron, the man for whom these garments are designed, is below making a golden calf (chapter 32). The garments are finally made in chapter 39.
historical:
The setting is Israel's encampment at Sinai in the months after the exodus, whose date is debated (see the note on chapter 13). Many modern scholars assign the tabernacle chapters to a priestly source and think they reflect, at least in part, the priesthood and worship of the Jerusalem temple in a later period; others hold that the account preserves genuine early traditions of a portable desert sanctuary, pointing to portable tent-shrines known from elsewhere in the ancient world. The garments described here continued to shape the high priest's dress for centuries; the first-century Jewish historian Josephus describes the high priest of his own day wearing the ephod, breastpiece, blue robe with bells, and gold plate.

The materials were costly. Blue and purple dyes were produced from marine snails along the eastern Mediterranean coast, in a slow and expensive process, which is why purple became a royal color across the ancient world. Scarlet dye came from an insect (the Hebrew phrase behind it includes the word for worm). Gold, fine linen, and engraved gemstones signaled that these garments belonged to a royal and sacred service.
cultural:
Priests in the ancient Near East wore special dress, and garments marked office and status just as uniforms do today. What stands out here is what the high priest's clothing carries. The two onyx stones on his shoulders and the twelve stones on his breastpiece bear the names of Israel's tribes, engraved like a seal. When Aaron entered the Holy Place, he literally carried the people on his shoulders and over his heart. The seal comparison is apt: a seal represented its owner, as Judah's did in Genesis 38.

The Urim and Thummim were placed in the breastpiece. The text never describes them, and their exact nature is uncertain, but other passages show they were used to learn God's will in a matter, apparently giving yes-or-no or chosen answers (Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 14:41 in the Greek version; Ezra 2:63). The words are often explained as meaning something like lights and perfections, though that too is debated. The identification of the twelve gems is also uncertain; ancient names for stones don't map neatly onto modern ones, which is why translations differ. The linen undergarments reflect a concern for modesty at the altar, already expressed in 20:26, and set Israel's worship apart from fertility rites in which nakedness had a religious role.
literary: The chapter is a set of building instructions, and its style is precise and repetitive, like a craftsman's specification. It begins with a list of six garments (verse 4) and then takes them roughly in order, spending most of its attention on the high priest's outer garments and moving from the ephod to the breastpiece, the robe, the gold plate, and finally the simpler garments for Aaron and his sons. Key phrases recur like a refrain: "glory and splendor" (verses 2 and 40), "a memorial" or "reminder before the LORD" (verses 12 and 29), "over his heart" (verses 29-30), "continually" (verses 29, 30, and 38), and the warning "so that he will not die" (verse 35, echoed in verse 43). The instructions are repeated almost word for word when the garments are made in chapter 39, a pattern of command and fulfillment that shows obedience carried out exactly.

outline.t: Aaron and his sons, and the holy garments
The ephod and its shoulder stones
The breastpiece of judgment, the twelve stones, and the Urim and Thummim
The blue robe with pomegranates and bells
The gold plate: HOLY TO THE LORD

doctrines.note: Everything about these garments says that approaching God is serious. The plate on the high priest's forehead reads HOLY TO THE LORD, and the repeated warning "so that he will not die" shows that God's holiness is not a small thing to be approached carelessly.

Verse 38 says Aaron will "bear the iniquity of the holy things", so that the people's gifts are acceptable to God despite their imperfection. The high priest stands as one who carries the people's guilt before God.

The priest bears the names of all twelve tribes, not just his own. The people come before God as one people, represented by one mediator, which the New Testament applies to the people of God gathered in Christ.

words.note: Ephod, a priestly garment, apparently a kind of apron or vest held by shoulder straps and a waistband. The word elsewhere can refer to a simple linen garment (1 Samuel 2:18) or to an object used in seeking God's guidance, and in Judges 8:27 an ephod becomes an idol. Here it is the base garment to which the breastpiece is attached.

Choshen, breastpiece, called the breastpiece of judgment (or decision) because it held the Urim and Thummim used for seeking God's decisions. Worn over the heart, it joins two things: carrying the people before God and seeking God's word for the people.

Zikkaron, memorial or reminder. The shoulder stones and the breastpiece are "a memorial before the LORD", as if God is being reminded of his people whenever the priest comes before him. The language is not that God forgets but that the priest's work is to hold the people before him.

Nasa, to lift or carry, in the sense of bearing guilt. The verb is used for Aaron bearing the names on his shoulders and heart (verses 12, 29) and bearing the iniquity of the holy things (verse 38). The same verb can mean both to carry a burden and to forgive, which is why it becomes important in the language of atonement (see 34:7).

christ: The New Testament's letter to the Hebrews reads Israel's priesthood as a pattern pointing to Christ, whom it calls "a great high priest" (Hebrews 4:14). Aaron bore the names of the tribes on his shoulders and over his heart; Hebrews says Christ is able to save completely those who come to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25). Aaron needed to be clothed and protected before he could approach God; Hebrews stresses that Christ, unlike Aaron, had no sin of his own to offer for (Hebrews 7:26-27). The book of Revelation describes the risen Christ in a long robe with a golden sash (Revelation 1:13), and the gemstones of this chapter reappear in the foundations of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:19-20). Peter calls the church "a royal priesthood" (1 Peter 2:9), so that what once belonged to one family is now extended, through Christ, to all his people. The connection is typological: the New Testament reads the priesthood as a pattern, not as a hidden prediction.

hard.q: Why does the Bible spend so much detail on clothing, and why the warnings of death?
hard.a: Modern readers often find these chapters tedious, and the warnings "so that he will not die" can seem out of proportion to the subject. The detail makes sense once one sees that the tabernacle and its priesthood are the answer to the central problem of Exodus: how a holy God can live among a sinful people without destroying them. Every part of the garments teaches something about that problem and its answer, from the names carried over the priest's heart to the gold plate that bears the people's imperfect offerings. The warnings are not arbitrary threats but a way of saying that holiness is real and dangerous to the unholy, a point the story makes vividly when Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu die after offering unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10:1-2). Some interpreters stress that the bells let the people outside know the priest was still alive and ministering; others see them as a way of announcing his approach to God. The text says only that the sound was to be heard so that he would not die.

questions: Aaron carried the names of the tribes on his shoulders and over his heart. Whom do you carry before God in prayer, and whom might you be forgetting?
The high priest wore HOLY TO THE LORD on his forehead. What would it mean for your daily work and appearance to belong to God in that way?
These garments were made for Aaron, who soon failed badly at the golden calf. How does it help to know that God's provision for worship doesn't depend on perfect people?
